title: Research
text: I study how the digital traces students leave in online learning environments can be turned into meaningful, theory-informed evidence about how they learn, so that educators can see and support self-regulated learning as it happens.

title: Research
text:
Current project

PhD research · The University of Western Australia · 2020–present

A systematic framework for context- and domain-driven event abstraction in multi-modal data within online collaborative learning environments
Learning platforms record every click, submission and forum post, but these low-level events say little on their own about whether a student is planning, monitoring or reflecting. My doctoral research develops a framework that abstracts raw, multi-modal event logs into high-level learning actions grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) theory and the course context. The resulting action sequences are analysed with process mining to reveal how students regulate their learning over time, and are validated through expert judgement.


Raw event logs
LMS, forums, code repositories


Event abstraction
context and domain rules


Learning actions
mapped to SRL phases


Process mining
sequences and patterns


Insight for educators
feedback and nudges


Research questions

How can low-level learning events be abstracted into learning actions that are meaningful from an SRL perspective?
How can course context and domain knowledge guide that abstraction across different learning environments?
What do the resulting process models reveal about how students regulate their learning in collaborative online settings?

title: The Syntax Trap: Re-evaluating Programming Pedagogy in Higher Education
text:
The pervasive challenge of programming education in higher institutions, despite its critical role in equipping future innovators, remains a significant concern. Having dedicated over a decade to teaching programming, my observations and experiences as a Computer Science Education PhD student compel me to critique the prevailing pedagogical approach: an overemphasis on programming language syntax at the expense of cultivating computational thinking. This deeply ingrained flaw in our curriculum frequently leads to a disheartening paradox: students who are fluent in syntax yet struggle profoundly with solving genuine computational problems.
The current paradigm, unfortunately, often treats programming as a linguistic exercise rather than a problem-solving discipline. Syllabi are frequently structured around an exhaustive tour of language constructs – variables, data types, control flow, functions, objects, and so forth. While undeniably foundational, this atomistic approach dissects the “how” of coding without adequately addressing the “why” or, crucially, the “what next.” Students diligently memorize keywords, understand operator precedence, and even master complex library functions. They can flawlessly write code that compiles and runs, yet when confronted with a novel problem requiring a decomposition into smaller, manageable parts, pattern recognition, abstraction, or algorithmic design, they often hit an insurmountable wall. Their mental toolkit is replete with hammers and screwdrivers, but they lack the blueprint or the architect’s vision to construct a building.
Computational thinking, in essence, is the cognitive process involved in formulating problems and their solutions in a way that is amenable to execution by a computer. It encompasses decomposition, breaking down complex problems into smaller, more manageable ones; pattern recognition, identifying similarities among and within problems; abstraction, focusing on the important information while ignoring irrelevant details; and algorithmic thinking, developing step-by-step solutions. These are the intellectual muscles that empower a programmer to translate a real-world challenge into an efficient and elegant computational solution. However, current teaching methodologies often sideline these crucial cognitive skills, implicitly assuming they will magically emerge from mere exposure to syntax.
This pedagogical oversight manifests in several critical ways. Students become reliant on rote memorization and pattern matching to previously seen examples, rather than developing the ability to analyze and synthesize. When faced with an unfamiliar problem, they lack the conceptual frameworks to approach it systematically. Debugging, a vital aspect of programming, becomes an exercise in trial and error rather than logical deduction, as they struggle to trace the flow of execution or reason about the underlying logic. Furthermore, this syntax-heavy approach often stifles creativity and intrinsic motivation. Programming transforms from an exciting endeavor of creation and problem-solving into a tedious task of adhering to rigid rules, leading to disengagement and a higher attrition rate in advanced courses.
The consequences of this imbalance are far-reaching. Graduates, despite holding degrees in Computer Science, may struggle in industry roles that demand adaptive problem-solving, innovative design, and the ability to work with ill-defined problems. They might possess the technical vocabulary but lack the fluency to converse in the language of solutions. This gap between academic training and industry demands creates a significant hurdle for both individuals and the broader technological landscape.
To rectify this imbalance, a fundamental shift in our educational philosophy is imperative. We must re-center our programming curricula around computational thinking, integrating it explicitly and implicitly throughout all levels of instruction. This means moving beyond merely demonstrating syntax and instead prioritizing activities that foster decomposition, abstraction, and algorithmic design. Early courses should introduce problem-solving strategies, perhaps through unplugged activities or visual programming environments, before diving headfirst into complex syntactical structures. Projects should be designed not just to test syntax mastery but to challenge students to apply computational thinking principles to solve real-world problems, even if simplified. Emphasis should be placed on code readability, logical correctness, and efficiency, rather than just functional output. Debugging should be taught as a systematic process of hypothesis testing and logical reasoning.
In conclusion, while programming language syntax is the vehicle, computational thinking is the engine that drives true problem-solving in computer science. Our current educational approach, with its undue focus on the former, is inadvertently producing a generation of skilled typists rather than adept problem solvers. It is time for a paradigm shift, one that prioritizes the cultivation of robust computational thinking skills alongside syntactical proficiency, ensuring that our graduates are not merely fluent in the language of computers, but are truly capable of harnessing their power to innovate and address the complex challenges of the 21st century.

title: Information overload is not a new phenomenom
text: Information overload is a real and present problem for many people. The constant bombardment of new information from technology and the ever-increasing speed of life can be overwhelming. This overload can lead to decreased productivity, decreased quality of work, and even depression. There are a few things that can be done to combat information overload. One is to be more selective about the sources of information that are allowed into one’s life. Another is to take breaks from technology and give the mind time to rest. Finally, it is important to learn how to effectively filter and process information. The first step to combating information overload is to be more selective about the sources of information that are allowed into one’s life. It is important to be intentional about what information is let in. Turn off notifications for email, social media, and news apps. Choose one or two sources for news and information that are trustworthy and stick with them. Be more selective about who you follow on social media and what you allow into your feed. The second step to combating information overload is to take breaks from technology and give the mind time to rest. Go for a walk, read a book, or take a break from screens altogether. Resist the urge to check email, social media, or the news every few minutes. Give yourself permission to disconnect from the constant flow of information. The third step to combating information overload is to learn how to effectively filter and process information. When presented with a deluge of information, it can be helpful to have some sort of system for sifting through it all. One method is to prioritize information based on urgency and importance. Another method is to chunk information into manageable pieces. By learning how to effectively filter and process information, we can lessen the negative impact of information overload in our lives.

title: Efficiency requires consitency of action
text: It is important to note that consistency is crucial for the success of a task, as it ensures that the desired outcome is achieved in a reliable and repeatable manner. Without consistency, even the most well-crafted initiative for improvement will fall short of its potential. In other words, for an action to be truly efficient, it must not only be performed with a high degree of skill, but also with a consistent level of adherence to established protocols and procedures.

title: Muhammad Azani Hasibuan
text:
I study how the digital traces students leave behind can be turned into insight that helps them learn. My work sits at the intersection of learning analytics, self-regulated learning and process mining.
I am a lecturer in Information Systems and a PhD candidate in Computer Science at the University of Western Australia. My doctoral research develops a framework that transforms low-level student activity logs into meaningful, theory-informed learning actions, so that educators can see and support self-regulated learning in online and collaborative environments. To do this, I combine process mining, machine learning and behavioural analytics with learning-science theory.
In the classroom, I design student-centred courses built on real-world case studies, mastery-based learning and active learning. I have taught Object-Oriented Programming, Databases and Information Systems Strategy, and my goal is always to make abstract concepts concrete and applicable.

title: Illusion of free time
text:
Close your eyes, and see how many times in your life when you had a lot of free time and you planned to do things that would make you better. For example, finishing some book you bought and never opened, writing a book, writing a paper, creating a website, etc.
These big projects seem promising at first. Then you start comparing what book you should read first, or what topic you should write about, or what technology you should use in your web project. And as time goes by, you spend most of your time on these kinds of activities. When the free time is running out, you realise that you haven’t started the actual task.
Then you realise, there is not enough time to do what you had planned. Then you get angry at yourself. This cycle may happen from time to time in your life. This phenomenon is called the “illusion and curse of leisure”.

title: New layer in luhmann’s slip box
text:
Card note-taking systems are not a new approach to note-taking from reading. Long before digital note apps, scholars copied quotations, facts and ideas onto index cards, one idea per card, and filed them in boxes. Guides such as Goutor’s (1980) The Card-File System of Note-Taking taught students to do exactly this when preparing essays and theses.
Niklas Luhmann, the German sociologist, used cards too. Yet his Zettelkasten, or slip box, is remembered not because it contained cards but because of what he did between the cards. He added a new layer to the old method: a way for cards to communicate with each other (Luhmann 1981).

title: New layer in luhmann’s slip box
text:
Card note-taking systems are not a new approach to note-taking from reading. Long before digital note apps, scholars copied quotations, facts and ideas onto index cards, one idea per card, and filed them in boxes. Guides such as Goutor’s (1980) The Card-File System of Note-Taking taught students to do exactly this when preparing essays and theses.
Niklas Luhmann, the German sociologist, used cards too. Yet his Zettelkasten, or slip box, is remembered not because it contained cards but because of what he did between the cards. He added a new layer to the old method: a way for cards to communicate with each other (Luhmann 1981).

title: New layer in luhmann’s slip box
text:
2 The classic card-file method
The card-file method rests on two strengths. The first is atomicity: each card holds a single idea, quotation or fact, so it can be understood on its own. The second is flexibility: because the cards are loose, they can be shuffled, grouped and regrouped. When writing, the scholar pulls out every card filed under a theme, spreads them on a desk, and arranges them into the order of an argument.
The weakness lies in how the cards are stored. In the classic system each card receives a subject heading or code, and it lives in the drawer for that subject (Figure 1). A card about “feedback” sits under Assessment; a card about “motivation” sits under Psychology. The cards are atomic and flexible, but they are also isolated. Any connection between them exists only in the writer’s head, and only at the moment of writing.






flowchart TB
  subgraph A["Assessment"]
    a1["Card: feedback timing"]
    a2["Card: rubrics"]
  end
  subgraph P["Psychology"]
    p1["Card: motivation"]
    p2["Card: self-efficacy"]
  end
  subgraph T["Technology"]
    t1["Card: learning dashboards"]
  end
  classDef card fill:#ffffff,stroke:#7a8699,color:#1f2d3d
  class a1,a2,p1,p2,t1 card
  style A fill:#eef3fb,stroke:#9fb3d1,color:#1f2d3d
  style P fill:#eef3fb,stroke:#9fb3d1,color:#1f2d3d
  style T fill:#eef3fb,stroke:#9fb3d1,color:#1f2d3d




Figure 1: Classic card file: cards are stored in topical silos. Connections across silos are not recorded.

title: New layer in luhmann’s slip box
text:
3 Luhmann’s new layer: connection
Luhmann kept some 90,000 cards over four decades, and he credited the slip box as a partner in producing dozens of books and hundreds of articles (Schmidt 2016). Two design choices made this possible.
First, he gave every card a fixed, branching number instead of a subject code. A new card was placed directly behind the card it most closely continued. If card 21/3 already had a successor 21/4, a new thought on 21/3 became 21/3a, and a comment on that became 21/3a1. The box could grow inward at any point, forever, without reorganisation. Position no longer meant “this belongs to topic X”; it meant “this continues that thought”.
Second, and more importantly, he linked cards. Whenever he wrote a card, he noted the numbers of other related cards, however distant in the box. A card on feedback could point to one on motivation and another on dashboards, even though they had been written years apart. A small keyword index then provided a handful of entry points into these chains, rather than a complete catalogue (Figure 2).






flowchart LR
  K(["Keyword index: 'feedback'"]) --> c1
  c1["21/3<br/>feedback timing"] --> c2["21/3a<br/>delayed feedback helps retention"]
  c2 --> c3["21/3a1<br/>but hurts novice motivation"]
  c1 --> c4["21/4<br/>feedback from peers"]
  c3 -.-> m1["57/12<br/>motivation and self-efficacy"]
  c4 -.-> d1["88/2c<br/>learning dashboards as feedback"]
  d1 -.-> m1




Figure 2: Luhmann’s slip box: branching numbers keep a line of thought together, while cross-references (dashed) connect ideas across distant parts of the box. A sparse keyword index offers entry points.

title: New layer in luhmann’s slip box
text:
4 Why the links matter
Links change what the box can do. In a silo system, you retrieve what you filed; you get back exactly what you expected. In a linked system, following a reference from one card leads to another you had forgotten, and from there to a third. Luhmann described the box as a communication partner because it could surprise him: it offered combinations of ideas that he had not planned (Luhmann 1981).
The links also move thinking earlier in the process. Deciding where a new card belongs and which cards it should point to forces you to ask how the idea relates to what you already know. That act is itself a form of reflection. Writing, then, becomes less about staring at a blank page and more about following and assembling chains of thought that already exist (Ahrens 2017).
Figure 3 summarises the difference as a workflow: the classic method ends with filing, while Luhmann’s method adds a step of connecting, and that step feeds directly into writing.






flowchart LR
  R["Read"] --> N["Write an atomic card"]
  N --> F["File by topic"]
  F -. classic method .-> W1["Collect cards by topic<br/>when writing"]
  N --> L["Place next to closest card<br/>and link related cards"]
  L --> I["Add keyword entry point"]
  I --> W2["Follow chains of links<br/>to build an argument"]
  style L fill:#2f6fdb,color:#fff,stroke:#2f6fdb




Figure 3: From reading to writing: the connecting step is the layer Luhmann added.

title: New layer in luhmann’s slip box
text:
5 Conclusion
The card, the drawer and the principle of one idea per note were already well established when Luhmann began. His contribution was a layer of connection on top of them. Instead of storing cards in silos or classifying them by code or label, he let each card refer to others and allowed the network, not the category, to carry meaning. For anyone taking notes today, whether on paper or in a digital tool, the lesson is the same: the value of a note depends less on where you file it than on what you connect it to.

title: New layer in luhmann’s slip box
text:

title: Writing habit is the key
text:
Ask a group of academics why they have not finished the paper they started last year and the answer is almost always the same: I don’t have time. Teaching, supervision, meetings and administration fill the week, so writing is postponed to the semester break, the weekend, or that mythical free month that never arrives. The assumption behind this answer is that good writing needs long, uninterrupted blocks of time.
Study after study shows that the assumption is wrong. You do not need much time to write effectively (Boice 1982, 1992; Krashen 2002). Writers who write a little almost every day produce more manuscripts than those who wait weeks or months between sessions. Writing just thirty minutes a day can make you one of those people who quietly publish several journal articles a year.

title: Writing habit is the key
text:
Ask a group of academics why they have not finished the paper they started last year and the answer is almost always the same: I don’t have time. Teaching, supervision, meetings and administration fill the week, so writing is postponed to the semester break, the weekend, or that mythical free month that never arrives. The assumption behind this answer is that good writing needs long, uninterrupted blocks of time.
Study after study shows that the assumption is wrong. You do not need much time to write effectively (Boice 1982, 1992; Krashen 2002). Writers who write a little almost every day produce more manuscripts than those who wait weeks or months between sessions. Writing just thirty minutes a day can make you one of those people who quietly publish several journal articles a year.

title: Writing habit is the key
text:
2 What the evidence shows
The clearest demonstration comes from psychologist Robert Boice, who spent years studying how university faculty actually write. In one experiment, he randomly assigned struggling academic writers to three conditions (Boice 1983). The first group, abstinence, was asked not to write except in emergencies. The second, spontaneous, scheduled writing sessions but wrote only when they felt inspired. The third, contingency management, scheduled daily sessions and was required to write in each one, with a mild penalty if they skipped.
The differences were striking (Figure 1). The contingency group wrote about 3.2 pages per day, compared with 0.9 pages for the spontaneous group and 0.2 pages for the abstinent group: sixteen times more output than not writing, and three and a half times more than waiting for the muse (Silvia 2007). Just as important, the forced writers did not become mechanical. They reported a new creative idea roughly every day, while the spontaneous writers reported one every two days and the abstinent writers one every five days. Krashen’s (2002) re-analysis of the same data confirmed the pattern and suggested that the gains came from regularity rather than from sheer volume.











(a) Mean pages written per day











(b) Median days between new creative ideas (lower is better)







Figure 1: Output and idea generation under three writing conditions, as reported by Boice (1983) and summarised by Silvia (2007).



Boice’s later work with new faculty told the same story (Boice 1992). The “quick starters” who thrived in their first years were not the ones with the lightest teaching loads. They were the ones who wrote in brief, regular sessions, often no more than an hour, and who stopped before they were exhausted. Binge writers, by contrast, reported more stress, more procrastination and, over time, fewer publications.

title: Writing habit is the key
text:
3 Why small and regular works
Several mechanisms explain the effect. First, a daily session keeps the project warm. When you return to a draft the next day, the argument is still in your head, so you spend your minutes writing rather than re-reading and re-orienting. After a two-month gap, the first week is lost to remembering what you meant.
Second, regular writing lowers the emotional stakes of any single session. If you write only once a month, that session has to be brilliant, and the pressure feeds perfectionism and avoidance. If you write every day, a weak session is just one of many, and it is easy to try again tomorrow.
Third, writing is thinking. Ideas do not arrive fully formed and wait to be typed; they emerge while we draft, revise and connect notes. This is why Boice’s scheduled writers generated more ideas, not fewer. Inspiration tends to follow the work.

title: Writing habit is the key
section: 4 What thirty minutes a day adds up to
text:
4 What thirty minutes a day adds up to
Small numbers compound. Suppose you write for thirty minutes, five days a week, and produce a modest 250 words per session. Figure 2 shows the cumulative result over a working year of 48 weeks.








Figure 2: Illustrative projection: cumulative draft words from 30 minutes a day (250 words per session, 5 sessions per week, 48 working weeks). Dashed lines mark the length of a typical 8,000-word journal article.





By the end of the year you would have drafted 60,000 words, enough raw material for seven full-length articles. Even if half of those words are cut in revision, the output still exceeds what most binge writers manage. The projection is deliberately conservative; it assumes no weekends, no writing retreats and no particularly good days.

title: Writing habit is the key
text:
5 Conclusion
The lesson is simple but easy to ignore: productive writing is less about talent or free time than about habit. Schedule a short session, treat it like a class you have to teach, and protect it. Start with thirty minutes. Write even when you do not feel like it, and stop when the time is up. The pages, and the ideas, will accumulate faster than you expect.

title: Writing habit is the key
text:
References


Boice, Robert. 1982. “Increasing the Writing Productivity of "Blocked" Academicians.” Behaviour Research and Therapy 20 (3): 197–207. https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-7967(82)90138-X.


Boice, Robert. 1983. “Contingency Management in Writing and the Appearance of Creative Ideas: Implications for the Treatment of Writing Blocks.” Behaviour Research and Therapy 21 (5): 537–43. https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-7967(83)90045-8.


Boice, Robert. 1992. The New Faculty Member: Supporting and Fostering Professional Development. Jossey-Bass.


Krashen, Stephen. 2002. “Optimal Levels of Writing Management: A Re-Analysis of Boice (1983).” Education 122 (3): 605–8.


Silvia, Paul J. 2007. How to Write a Lot: A Practical Guide to Productive Academic Writing. American Psychological Association.

title: Learning Analytics in the Age of AI: Reflections from a Computing Educator
text:
When I first started teaching programming over a decade ago, my biggest concern was how to keep students engaged beyond the syntax. Why did some students thrive while others got lost after the second loop? How could I identify students struggling with core concepts before they failed their exams?
Fast forward to today — we’re living in an era where data from every keystroke, click, submission, and discussion thread is logged. Our classrooms, especially in computer science, are rich with digital traces of learning. The challenge now is not collecting data, but making sense of it. This is where Learning Analytics (LA) comes in — and in the age of Artificial Intelligence, it’s becoming a game changer.

title: Learning Analytics in the Age of AI: Reflections from a Computing Educator
text:
🎯 So, What Is Learning Analytics?
In simple terms, learning analytics is about measuring and analyzing student data to understand and improve learning. It’s not a new idea, but the capabilities have grown exponentially. Today, we can track not just whether a student submitted an assignment, but how they coded it, how long they spent on debugging, which resources they consulted, and whether they learned deeply or just barely enough to get by.
In my classes, especially those involving Java, GitHub, or Moodle-based labs, I can now access a full behavioral footprint. It’s like having a mirror that shows how my students actually learn — not just what they score.

title: Learning Analytics in the Age of AI: Reflections from a Computing Educator
section: 🤖 Why the AI Era Changes Everything
text:
🤖 Why the AI Era Changes Everything
The hype around AI often centers on large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT or tools like GitHub Copilot. But for educators, the real transformation is in how AI enables new layers of interpretation and prediction in learning analytics.
Here’s what AI makes possible:

Pattern detection: Algorithms can identify students who are silently disengaging long before it becomes visible to a lecturer.
Personalized feedback: AI systems can provide individualized nudges based on how a student learns, not just what they got wrong.
Cognitive modeling: We’re getting closer to modeling students’ self-regulated learning — things like planning, monitoring, and reflecting — by interpreting multimodal data (LMS logs, GitHub commits, Slack messages, etc.).

For those of us in Computing Education, where the learning process is as important as the output (i.e., code), this is gold.

title: Learning Analytics in the Age of AI: Reflections from a Computing Educator
section: 🎓 The Higher Ed Reality: Promise and Pitfalls
text:
🎓 The Higher Ed Reality: Promise and Pitfalls
Let’s be honest: most universities are still catching up. Sure, we have LMS dashboards and performance reports, but they’re mostly descriptive. Very few institutions use LA proactively — to intervene, to mentor, to redesign.
I’ve seen three common pitfalls:

Data without pedagogy: Just because we can measure doesn’t mean we’re asking the right questions.
Surveillance over support: Students are more likely to accept analytics if it helps them grow, not just monitor them.
Lack of faculty training: Many educators are still wary or unaware of what LA (and AI) can offer.

We need a cultural shift where learning analytics becomes part of the instructional design, not just an admin add-on.

title: Learning Analytics in the Age of AI: Reflections from a Computing Educator
section: 🧠 Case in Point: My Current Research
text:
🧠 Case in Point: My Current Research
My own PhD journey is centered around this question: Can we transform raw log data into meaningful indicators of student learning behavior? I’m working on a framework that abstracts low-level events — like assignment-view, quiz-start, code-push — into high-level learning actions using domain knowledge and context (e.g., early planning, deadline-driven cramming, iterative coding).
One of the most exciting directions? Using supervised learning and expert validation to map these behaviors to dimensions of self-regulated learning. The end goal is to give students a mirror — not to shame them, but to guide them.

title: Learning Analytics in the Age of AI: Reflections from a Computing Educator
section: 🌱 What Can We Do as Educators?
text:
🌱 What Can We Do as Educators?
If you’re a fellow CS educator, here are a few humble suggestions:

Start small: Use your LMS logs to identify common drop-off points. When do students stop engaging?
Visualize: Plot timelines of activity — are students coding steadily or all in the last 24 hours?
Reflect: Share anonymized patterns with your students. Ask: What kind of learner are you becoming?
Collaborate: Work with learning scientists or data analysts at your institution. You don’t have to do it alone.

title: Learning Analytics in the Age of AI: Reflections from a Computing Educator
text:
✨ Final Thoughts
Learning Analytics in the AI era isn’t about replacing educators. It’s about augmenting our ability to care, support, and design better learning experiences. As computing educators, we are uniquely positioned — not only to teach about AI but to use it to transform how our students learn to learn.
In the end, the best analytics system is not the one that predicts grades. It’s the one that helps a struggling student find their way back into the joy of learning.
Let’s build that future — mindfully, ethically, and with our students at the center.

title: The aim of note-taking
text:
The purpose of taking note is to help us thinking in a visible way. In reading, it helps us to test our understanding about the text. This self-testing itself is a type of reflective activity. Hence the note-taking in reading is a visible reflective thinking.
Our notes should contain the key and significant idea.
